On a fresh PropertyListSerializer (objsToIds empty), id(of: A) with A.objectID == "OBJ_2" returns "\"OBJ_2\"" and objsToIds.count becomes 1. Then id(of: B), for a distinct B (A !== B) whose objectID is nil, computes "OBJ_\(1 + 1)" and returns "\"OBJ_2\"" again. Harness output: `direct: id(of: A[objectID OBJ_2]) = "OBJ_2"  id(of: B[nil]) = "OBJ_2"  A !== B: true  equal results: true`.

It is also reachable through the public API alone (Xcode.Project(), addTarget(objectID:name:) and generatePlist() are all public). Project() plus addTarget(objectID: "OBJ_7", name: "T") assigns ids in this order: project OBJ_1, project build settings OBJ_2, Debug OBJ_3, Release OBJ_4, mainGroup OBJ_5, then the target with custom id "OBJ_7" (count goes to 6). The target's own build settings then get "OBJ_\(6 + 1)" = OBJ_7, a second distinct object with the same id. serialize(object:) finds idsToDicts["\"OBJ_7\""] already holding the target's sentinel:
- release (-O): generatePlist throws `InternalError("tried to serialize Xcode.BuildSettingsTable twice")`.
- debug (-Onone): the process traps on the assertionFailure in InternalError.init.
With objectID "OBJ_2" the run throws "tried to serialize Xcode.Target twice".

Corrected variant through the real default: two targets with the same name, addTarget(name: "ALL") twice. Both get custom id "TARGET_ALL" (distinct keys, equal results), and generatePlist throws or traps the same way.

Side finding, confirmed by running it: FileReference.objectID is never consulted. addFileReference(objectID: "FILE_CUSTOM") yields fref.objectID == "FILE_CUSTOM", but id(of: fref) == "\"OBJ_1\"". Target.objectID is honoured: id(of: target) == "\"TARGET_T\"".

XcodeProjectModelSerialization.swift @ e739e651:
- L478 `let serObjRef = SerializedObjectRef(object)`. Equality and hashing are object identity (L455-461), so A and B are distinct keys.
- L479-481: the memo lookup misses for a new object.

bd.contract_reason:
The owner's documentation pulls two ways:
- The protocol requirement's doc (L557-559) says: "A custom ID to use for the instance, if enabled. This ID must be unique across the entire serialized graph." Read literally, that puts the uniqueness burden on whoever supplies the custom id, so a custom "OBJ_2" that a generated id later duplicates breaks the documented requirement.
- The protocol doc also promises (L523-524) that "Every object that is written to the Serializer is assigned an id (an arbitrary but unique string)". The serializer itself chose B's "OBJ_2", so that promise is the serializer's.
- Nothing reserves or documents the "OBJ_<n>" namespace. The public entry points, addTarget(objectID:) and Target.objectID, carry no doc at all.

So a caller has no stated way to know which custom ids are safe. It is unclear rather than plainly forbidden. One unstated habit: every in-repo custom id carries a "TARGET_" prefix, which keeps it clear of "OBJ_".
bd.reachability_reason:
The judges' sequence is not reachable from this repository. Custom ids flow into L485 only from Xcode.Target; FileReference's objectID is dead because of the base-class conformance, as shown by running it.

Every in-repo addTarget call passes no objectID (ProjectGenerator.swift L54 "swift-include-substitutions", L107 "ALL", L297 generateBaseTarget, L844 "ninja-build-<exe>"). So every custom id is "TARGET_<name>", which can never equal a generated "OBJ_<n>". No caller passes objectID to addFileReference (L199), and no test touches objectID or generatePlist. Package.swift declares no library products, so SwiftXcodeGen's public API has no outside consumers beyond the swift-xcodegen executable and its tests.

The closest reachable relative is a different mechanism: two Target objects with the same name share "TARGET_<name>". generateBaseTarget dedupes names only against its `targets` dictionary, and the directly added "ALL", "swift-include-substitutions" and "ninja-build-<exe>" targets are never registered there. A Swift module or clang target named exactly "ALL" or "swift-include-substitutions" would therefore make generatePlist (ProjectGenerator L875) throw "tried to serialize Xcode.Target twice", or trap on the assertionFailure in a debug build of swift-xcodegen. No such target name is realistic in the swift repo, and the failure is loud, not a corrupt project file.

A silent wrong reference (an id(of:)-only alias) needs a custom "OBJ_<n>" id, which only a hypothetical external caller could supply.

bd.summary:
The witness holds, both by trace and by running it. id(of:) takes a custom objectID verbatim and generates "OBJ_\(count+1)" without checking either against ids already issued, so a custom "OBJ_2" and a later nil-objectID object both get "\"OBJ_2\"". Through the public addTarget(objectID:) and generatePlist() this makes generatePlist throw, or trap in debug builds.

It is not reachable in this repository: the only custom ids are "TARGET_<name>", and FileReference.objectID is never consulted. The owner's own docs conflict on who owns uniqueness, and the visible effect is a loud InternalError, not corrupt output, so this should be recorded as latent rather than filed. Worth a mention alongside it: two latent defects on the same main-branch code, FileReference.objectID being dead and the "ALL"/"swift-include-substitutions"/"ninja-build-*" targets bypassing the name dedupe.

bd.witness: Fresh Writer (nextID = 1). id("a1") returns "a11", and nextID becomes 2. Nine calls to id("b") return "b2" through "b10", and nextID becomes 11. id("a") then returns "a11" again, the same as the first call. I copied lines 93-96 verbatim into a standalone struct (<scratch>/669/handcheck/bd-7/repro/main.swift), compiled it with swiftc and ran it. It printed ["a11","b2",...,"b10","a11"] and equal: true. The same harness found no duplicates in 5000 interleaved calls that used only the two prefixes the real callers pass, "grad" and "shadow". I did not build the Graffle package itself. It is an AppKit app and Writer is private, so the reproduction runs on a transcription of the function body, not the package.
bd.trace: SVGExport.swift:89 `var nextID = 1`; :93-96 `mutating func id(_ prefix: String) -> String { defer { nextID += 1 }; return "\(prefix)\(nextID)" }`. The return value is the plain concatenation of prefix and counter, with no separator and no check against ids already issued. So prefix "a1" with counter 1 and prefix "a" with counter 11 both produce "a11". The only call sites are :133 `let gid = id("grad")` (in fillAttrs, for linear and radial gradients) and :171 `let fid = id("shadow")` (in shadowFilter).
bd.execution_note: I ran a transcription of the verbatim body of lines 93-96, compiled with swiftc, in the scratch directory. I did not build the Graffle package: Writer is a private nested struct in an AppKit app target, and the package has no test target that could reach it.
bd.contract_reason: id(_:) has no doc comment, and neither Writer nor SVGExport states a precondition on `prefix`, so nothing forbids a prefix ending in a digit. The callers do follow an unstated habit, though. Writer is `private` to SVGExport, and both call sites pass fixed literals that do not end in a digit ("grad" and "shadow"). Writer is also created fresh for every SVGExport.svg(for:bounds:) call (line 8).
bd.reachability_reason: The prefix is never user-controlled. The only callers are id("grad") at line 133 and id("shadow") at line 171, and no layer name, shape text, file content or theme value reaches the prefix. With those two digit-free literals the output is injective. For a single prefix, distinct counters give distinct decimal suffixes. Across the two prefixes, "grad…" and "shadow…" can never be equal, and neither can equal the document's other ids ("layer-…", "shape-…" and "connector-…", which all contain a hyphen). Each export (CanvasView.svgData(), line 2505, the single SVGExport.svg call site) builds one fresh Writer, so ids are never mixed across Writers. No user-visible duplicate id or wrong gradient/filter reference can come out of the current code. The defect would only become live if someone later added a call site whose prefix ends in a digit.

rows.how_a_test_builds_it: `@testable import SwiftCompilerPluginMessageHandling` (exposed as the underscored product `_SwiftCompilerPluginMessageHandling`; the class, its init, SourceManager and ParsedSyntaxRegistry are all internal), plus `import SwiftSyntax`: `PluginMacroExpansionContext(sourceManager: SourceManager(syntaxRegistry: ParsedSyntaxRegistry(cacheCapacity: 1)), lexicalContext: [], staticBuildConfiguration: nil)`. The discriminator defaults to "". Inputs are arbitrary Strings, so a generator is trivial. Compare `.text`, not the token: TokenSyntax `==` is node identity (SyntaxHashable.swift:23), so the law would hold vacuously.
rows.note: I agree it is a genuine per-receiver uniquifier. The counter `uniqueNames` is instance-owned and only grows, and nothing has to be called first. Output is D + "<name.count><name>fMu<idx-1?>_". Proof that it is injective for a fixed D: the trailing digit run before the final '_' is preceded by 'u', so the right end parses one way. If two count prefixes differed, the longer count would have to be at least 10 times the shorter one, but then name1 = (extra digits) + name2, which forces count1 >= count2. That is a contradiction. Canonically equivalent names ("\u{E9}" and "e\u{301}") share a Dictionary key, so they get different indices. "" maps to "__local" and shares its counter ("7__localfMu_", then "7__localfMu0_"). Executed against the real code at 4a71c31 (exported to scratch, built in 32s, package at <scratch>/669/handcheck/recheck-1/src/recheck-pkg). On fresh receivers I ran 117 adversarial fixed calls (names led by digits, names containing fMu/_, combining marks, Prepend, ZWJ, Hangul), 8 x 40,000 fuzzed calls, and 105,000 repeats of digit-led names. There were 0 collisions under String == and 0 at the UTF-8 byte level. Caveat: uniqueness holds only within one receiver. Across expansions it rests on the compiler-supplied discriminator, which the per-receiver law does not need. The Int overflow on `uniqueIndex + 1` cannot be reached.

rows.how_a_test_builds_it: Public API, no @testable needed: `BasicMacroExpansionContext()` (discriminator "__macro_local_") or `BasicMacroExpansionContext(expansionDiscriminator: "")`. Inputs are arbitrary Strings, so a generator is trivial. Compare `.text` (token == is node identity). Upstream already has a two-call instance in Tests/SwiftSyntaxMacroExpansionTest/MultiRoleMacroTests.swift:33-37 ("__macro_local_4minefMu_" and then "...fMu0_").
rows.note: The mangling and argument are the same as in the plugin context. The counter lives in `SharedState`, a private class instance created by each `init(...)`. It is not global or static. Only `init(sharingWith:)` shares it, which is not a fresh receiver. I confirmed by execution that a sharing context continues the counter ("__macro_local_1xfMu_" and then "__macro_local_1xfMu0_"), so it does not restart. Executed against the real code at 4a71c31 with the same battery: 117 fixed calls, 8 x 40,000 fuzzed calls with either default or empty discriminator, and 105,000 repeats of digit-led names. There were 0 collisions by String == and by bytes. The protocol doc (MacroExpansionContext.swift) promises "a unique name that will not conflict with any other name", and the doc on this type says it is for testing. The empty-name substitution is not a sentinel: it shares the "__local" counter and still yields distinct names.

rows.how_a_test_builds_it: `@testable import FoundationEssentials` (the repo's own tests do this, e.g. Tests/FoundationEssentialsTests/BufferViewTests.swift). The struct is `package` and its init and method are internal: `var state = DebugStringConversionState([])`, then `state.addCapture(v)` with any `Any`. An Any generator is trivial (Int/String/Bool/nil). The returned name does not depend on the value.
rows.note: It returns "capture\(nextCapture)" and a `defer` then increments the stored counter. The return value is taken before the defer runs, so a fresh state gives capture1, capture2, ... captureN. Nothing else writes `nextCapture`, and init sets it to 1. These are identifier names: captureDecl declares them, and the predicate description refers to them (PredicateTests.swift:528-533 expects capture1 and capture2). No doc comment states uniqueness. The contract is implicit from that role, which is the one soft spot. Execution: building the real package needs network-fetched deps (swift-collections, swift-foundation-icu, swift-syntax), so I compiled a verbatim copy of lines 13-54 against macOS Foundation instead. The only edits were `package` to internal and, in the unrelated subscript, `variable.id` to `variable`, because `id` is internal. 26,000 calls over nil, Bool, Int, a String with quotes, Date, Data, UUID, a type whose description contains a newline, an array, a Double, the String "capture1" and Int.max gave 26,000 distinct names, exactly capture1...capture26000 (copy at <scratch>/669/handcheck/recheck-1/foundation-copy/main.swift). Overflow would need 2^63 calls.

rows.how_a_test_builds_it: `@testable import SwiftUMLBridgeFramework`; `var ids = DiagramIdentifiers(sanitize: DepsScript.mermaidId)`. Any `(String) -> String` closure works, and both real sanitizers are internal statics reachable with @testable. Then call `id(forKey:sanitizing:)` on a generated `[(key: String, text: String)]` drawn from a narrow alphabet that collides under the sanitizer (for example "a", "_", ".", "-", "a_2"). A generator is plausible. The repo's own `distinctNamesGetDistinctIdentifiers` test already checks the one-argument form exhaustively for names up to 3 characters.
rows.note: This is a real identifier-issuing table. `byKey` memoizes by key, so a repeated key returns the stored id and ignores the new `text`. A new key's candidate is checked against `taken` (every id issued so far) before it is inserted, so distinct keys always get distinct ids, whatever the sanitizer does. The loop ends because `taken` is finite. The struct and its init are internal; a fresh struct has nothing reserved and needs no other call first. Checked by executable reproduction against a verbatim copy of the struct, taken with `git show` at c6c82e3 (<scratch>/669/handcheck/recheck-2/replica/main.swift): every sequence of up to 4 (key, text) pairs from a 5x5 alphabet, under 6 sanitizers (identity, a constant "x", empty string, mermaidId, safeAlias, and an adversarial `$0 + "_2"`). That is 2,441,400 sequences and 0 violations of either half: equal keys gave equal ids, distinct keys gave distinct ids.

rows.counterexample: Only outside the contract, with a name that was not reserved: `NodeIdAllocator(reserving: [])` then issue "A", "A", "A_1" gives "A", "A_1", "A_1" (the same happens with reserving ["A"]). The first issue of a name returns the name unchecked against `taken`. In-contract inputs give no counterexample.
rows.how_a_test_builds_it: `@testable import SwiftUMLBridgeFramework`; `var alloc = LayoutGraphBuilder.NodeIdAllocator(reserving: R)`, where R is a generated `[String]` from a narrow, suffix-shaped alphabet ("A", "A_1", "A_2", "A_1_1", "B"). Then call `issue(for:)` on a sequence drawn from R with repeats, for example generated indices into R. This is a dependent generator, and it is plausible. A generator that draws inputs independently of R leaves the contract and finds the duplicate above.
rows.note: A real id-issuing allocator: the same name issued again gets a fresh `_n` id, so the law is n calls, n distinct ids, not memoization. The law holds only for inputs inside the reserved set. That restriction is the documented contract ("Every drawn element's name is reserved up front"), and the only caller keeps it: LayoutGraphBuilder.swift:22 reserves `entries.filter(\.isDrawn).map(\.name)`, and line 35 issues only for drawn entries. Here is why it holds. A suffixed id is chosen outside `taken` and then inserted, so it differs from every earlier id. A name's first issue returns the bare name x. Any earlier issue of x would have been either a first issue of x (impossible, since this is the first) or another name's suffixed id (impossible, since x was in `taken` from init). The reservation is the initialiser's argument, not a separate call, so I agree that setup is false. It does tie the input domain to the construction, which is borderline under the rubric. Checked by executable reproduction against the verbatim struct (same probe file): all 127 non-empty reserved subsets of a 7-name alphabet (including "" and suffix-shaped names), with every issue sequence of up to 5 names drawn from the subset. That is 228,704 sequences and 0 duplicates.

rows.counterexample: Only for names the recognizer cannot produce together: actions named "class" and "`class`" (any parameters) both return "`class`", because `unique` values differ but escapeIfKeyword maps "class" onto the second name's literal text. In the probe this was the only failure family: 113,440 failing sequences, every one containing a backticked name; there were 0 failures among 346,200 backtick-free sequences.
rows.how_a_test_builds_it: The function is `private static`, and @testable lifts only internal, not private or fileprivate, so a test cannot call it. The law can be stated one hop up through the public `ViewModelActionEnumEmitter.emit(typeName:actions:)`. That function makes a fresh empty `Set<String>` and calls uniqueCaseName once per admitted action. Build `[ViewModelAction]` with the public init, using isAsync: false and isThrows: false (skipped actions never reach the function). Draw names from a narrow alphabet ("add", "addX", "add2", "addUnlabeled") and labels from {nil, "x", "y"}. Then assert that `result.lifted.map(\.caseName)` is pairwise distinct. A generator is plausible; it must draw backtick-free names, or names in only one form per keyword.
rows.note: I agree with the judges on the verdict (UNIQUIFIER over a fresh inout Set) and on the body. I disagree only on expressible: the subject itself is private, so a test can state the law only on its public caller `emit`. Why the body keeps the law: every candidate, whether the bare name, the name plus labels, or a numbered form, is checked against `taken` and then inserted, so the unescaped `unique` values are pairwise distinct. Escaping is injective unless one name equals another's backticked keyword. In my probe, the probe's same-file wrapper agreed with `emit`'s lifted case names on all 637,420 sequences. Aside: the recognizer stores `node.name.text` (ViewModelDiscoveryVisitor.swift:151). swift-syntax's raw token text keeps backticks; its `Identifier` type exists to strip them. So the emitter's comment that names arrive stripped is wrong, and on recognizer output escapeIfKeyword never fires for a backticked keyword. Only one form of each keyword ever arrives, so the counterexample cannot happen in practice. One collision that the string law does not see: real source with `func `add`()` and `func add(x:)` yields the case names "`add`" and "add". Those are distinct strings but the same Swift identifier, so the emitted enum would declare duplicate cases. This needs a needlessly backticked non-keyword overload, which is exotic. Checked by executable reproduction against a verbatim copy of the emitter and of ViewModelAction, taken with `git show` at eea6466 (<scratch>/669/handcheck/recheck-2/replica/main.swift): every sequence of up to 4 actions from 7 names x 4 parameter shapes.
